analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred members of Congress and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, stock options, commodities, and similar financial instruments while in office. It allowed only diversified mutual funds, ETFs, federal retirement plan investments, and Treasury securities, plus assets in a qualified blind trust. Any profits from banned trades would have to be returned to the Treasury, with possible civil fines, and the ethics office would audit compliance every two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who want lawmakers deciding policy without personal bets on the outcomes. Members would have to put investments in diversified funds or blind trusts, and any profits from banned trades go to the Treasury, not the member.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens, and public trust in Congress

how_it_helps.text: Bans members and their spouses from holding or trading individual stocks, securities futures, commodities, and synthetic derivatives like options and warrants during their terms.
Allows only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, Thrift Savings Plan investments, and U.S. Treasury securities, and exempts holdings in a qualified blind trust.
Requires profits from prohibited trades to be disgorged to the Treasury, blocks tax deductions for losses on banned trades, and exposes violators to civil fines.
Requires annual compliance certifications from each member, posted on a public website, with audits by the supervising ethics office at least every two years.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to sell individual holdings or move them into blind trusts and give up trading access while in office.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Penalties are civil, not criminal: a violator repays profits and may face a fine, with no jail exposure in the bill itself.
The spouse-only family coverage leaves children, parents, and other relatives free to trade, and the qualified blind trust exception still allows a compliant path for large holdings.
Enforcement depends on the supervising ethics office issuing certifications and audits, which are administrative processes that could be under-resourced or unevenly applied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is stronger public confidence that lawmakers are not trading on information from their official duties, at little cost to anyone outside Congress. The design has real gaps, notably civil-only penalties and coverage limited to spouses, but the core restriction is straightforward and enforceable through disgorgement and audits.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Administration and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, neither committee took action, and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Zachary Nunn introduced the bill on February 21, 2023, joined by Rep. Greg Stanton as original cosponsor.
It was referred to the Committee on House Administration and the Committee on Ways and Means for consideration of provisions in their jurisdictions.
Five additional members cosponsored the bill, three Democrats and two Republicans, giving it sponsorship from both parties.
No further action was recorded; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress who wanted to keep buying and selling individual stocks and other securities while in office are better off, since no restrictions were enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members who kept their trading rights

for.name: Three additional cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on after introduction, giving the bill bipartisan support of five cosponsors.

against.name: Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Bryan Steil, R-WI)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Second committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Jason Smith, R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for provisions in its jurisdiction and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The six sponsors and cosponsors split three Republicans and three Democrats, but the record shows no committee or floor action, so no votes reveal how the full chamber would have split.

industries.note: The bill would have taken away members' and their spouses' ability to hold or trade individual stocks, options, and commodities during their terms, with profits from banned trades clawed back to the Treasury. Its failure leaves the current trading disclosure regime in place.
